title: India and the US Began Four Days of Trade Talks Today. The Real Fight Is Over Section 301.
excerpt: New Delhi wants protection from a separate US investigation that could slap additional tariffs on Indian goods. The current deal framework would lock India in at 18% — but only if it's signed before July 24.
body:
A high-level American delegation led by chief negotiator Brendan Lynch arrived in New Delhi on Monday for four days of talks that both sides describe as critical to finalising the contours of a landmark bilateral trade agreement. But according to Indian government sources speaking to Reuters, the real agenda goes beyond the deal itself.

India is seeking explicit protection from Washington's separate **Section 301 investigation** — a probe launched after the US Supreme Court struck down President Trump's sweeping reciprocal tariffs earlier this year. The outcome of these talks could determine whether Indian exporters face a manageable 18% tariff or something significantly worse.

## The Stakes

The trade relationship between the world's largest and fifth-largest economies has been building toward this moment since February, when both nations agreed on a framework for an interim bilateral trade agreement. Under that framework, the US would reduce tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18%, and India would drop its 25% penalty on Indian products linked to Russian oil purchases.

But the ground shifted on February 20, when the US Supreme Court ruled against Trump's reciprocal tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The White House pivoted to a blanket 10% tariff on all countries and simultaneously launched Section 301 investigations into 16 trading partners, including India.

Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 is the same legal mechanism Washington used to impose tariffs worth hundreds of billions of dollars on China during the late 2010s trade war. For India, the stakes are existential: being found in violation without a negotiated agreement in place could mean tariffs far above the 18% currently on the table.

## What India Wants

According to an Indian trade source who spoke on condition of anonymity, New Delhi's negotiating position centres on three objectives.

First, relief from any additional tariffs that might emerge from the Section 301 probe. Indian officials believe that signing the bilateral deal before the investigation concludes — the deadline is **July 24** — would effectively shield Indian exports from punitive duties.

Second, India is seeking **preferential tariff treatment relative to competing manufacturing hubs** in South and Southeast Asia. Specifically, New Delhi wants rates that give it an advantage over Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka as it tries to strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Third, India wants the terms to be "fair, equitable, and balanced," the source told Reuters — language that signals New Delhi will not accept a deal that merely codifies the current tariff imbalance.

## The Negotiating Teams

India's delegation is led by Darpan Jain, Additional Secretary in the Department of Commerce and the country's chief negotiator. The talks will cover market access, non-tariff measures, customs and trade facilitation, investment promotion, and what the Commerce Ministry calls "economic security alignment."

The discussions build on an April round held in Washington, where Jain's team met with American counterparts from April 20-23. The momentum has been sustained by diplomatic signals from both sides. US Ambassador Sergio Gor, speaking at the American Chamber of Commerce summit in Delhi last week, said he "fully expects the trade deal will be signed over the next few weeks and months" and noted that bilateral trade has grown from $20 billion to over $220 billion in two decades.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could visit India once the broad contours are agreed, a signal that both sides see the finish line.

## The Complications

The negotiations are not occurring in a vacuum. The US-Iran conflict has disrupted global energy markets, pushing up prices and creating new pressure points in the trade relationship. India's recent pivot to Venezuelan, Brazilian, and Angolan crude oil — forced by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — has added a new dimension to energy security discussions that will inevitably bleed into trade talks.

There is also the question of how much flexibility India has to reduce tariffs on American agricultural and industrial goods while protecting domestic producers. The February framework committed India to "significant purchases" of American energy and technology products, but the details remain unresolved.

## The NRI Angle

For the Indian diaspora — particularly the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans whose professional and financial lives straddle both economies — the deal's outcome will be felt directly. A bilateral trade agreement that locks in competitive tariff rates would benefit Indian IT services firms that serve American clients, Indian pharmaceutical companies that export generics to the US market, and the growing cohort of Indian manufacturers seeking to position themselves as China-plus-one alternatives for American companies.

The July 24 deadline gives both sides less than eight weeks to move from framework to legal text. Ambassador Gor offered a comparison: the EU and India have been negotiating their trade deal for almost 19 years. The US and India have been at it for about four months. The question is whether speed will produce a deal that sticks — or one that falls apart under its own ambition.
author: Diaspora Desk
